arguments.name: Habermas cites skeptics extensively in print
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
arguments.conclusion: Habermas is not avoiding or hiding skeptical scholars, because his published volumes cite thousands of sources across the ideological spectrum.
premises: P1: Volume 3 contains roughly 8,000 footnotes and cites scholars from evangelicals to atheists.
P2: Habermas's criterion for inclusion is a terminal degree in a relevant field, regardless of the scholar's religious stance.
P3: Critics who say he refuses to name skeptics largely have not read or cited his books.

st1.quote: So, I'm not hiding in any way from names.

st2.quote: Uh evangelicals to atheists. It's my definition is if you have a terminal degree in a relevant field and I think I list six or seven relevant fields.

st3.quote: Ben told me from his counting, Ben told me I think he said there's a little less than 8,000 footnotes in that book.

st4.quote: But if there's 8,000 footnotes, I think I'm doing some citing and it's across the board.

st5.quote: But you know, you already said it. These folks largely do not site the book cuz I got a feeling am I just naive that they didn't read it and they don't know.

st6.quote: So, I'm not hiding in any way from names.

st7.quote: If you start accounting, the critics have gotten it. It's not Habermass mentions them one or two times and goes off on them 400 times.

st8.quote: It's jam-packed with names and citations on page after page.

arguments.prior_art: Gary Habermas, The Historical Jesus (1996) / minimal facts method

or1.quote: So, I'm not hiding in any way from names.
or1.why: It is a self-defense variant of the standard Habermas minimal-facts citation practice, not a new historical argument.

or2.quote: Ben told me from his counting, Ben told me I think he said there's a little less than 8,000 footnotes in that book.
or2.why: The 8,000-footnote count and the terminal-degree inclusion rule are specific new support data.

or4.why: No formalization or model is added.

arguments.weakest_link: The claim that critics have not read the books is an inference about motive, not evidence.
arguments.develop_next: Provide an actual count or sample audit of skeptical vs. evangelical citations in volume 3.

arguments.name: Volume 3 was an add-on research tool, not an attack
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
arguments.conclusion: Volume 3 was originally an add-on bibliographic catch-up volume and was not written to attack or embarrass anyone.
premises: P1: Habermas originally planned only three volumes and began the project to update his bibliographic follow-up after 1975.
P2: Michael Licona suggested the 1,500 pages on people's views become a fourth volume, and the publisher immediately agreed.
P3: The volume is intended to help researchers, students, and podcasters quickly locate scholarly views and quotations.

st1.quote: So it was an add-on volume for me to catch up and Mike said throw it in there.

st2.quote: I was originally only going to do three volumes.

st3.quote: Michael Lona said to me, he said, "Hey, you've got these 1500 pages on people's views. I think that would interest a lot of people. Why don't you ask your publisher if they want that to be volume four?"

st4.quote: So, there was a lot of interest there.

st5.quote: I didn't write it with a view to upsetting somebody. Nothing like that.

st6.quote: But it has it has very little to do with blasting guys or giving arguments.

st7.why: No kill condition or test is given.

st8.quote: So I was doing it for me to refamiliarize myself with sources.

or1.quote: So it was an add-on volume for me to catch up and Mike said throw it in there.
or1.why: This is an autobiographical account of the volume's origin, not a restatement of a prior argument.

or2.quote: Michael Lona said to me, he said, "Hey, you've got these 1500 pages on people's views. I think that would interest a lot of people. Why don't you ask your publisher if they want that to be volume four?"
or2.why: The Licona/publisher origin story is new evidence not used in prior minimal-facts arguments.

arguments.weakest_link: The intention claim rests on Habermas's own testimony about his motives.
arguments.develop_next: Show the volume's introduction or publisher correspondence confirming the stated origin and purpose.

arguments.name: Fairness challenge to critics
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
arguments.conclusion: Critics who complain about his citation balance should produce a comparable work with the same percentage of opposing scholars cited fairly.
premises: P1: Critics allege that most of his footnotes are to evangelicals or scholars friendly to evangelicals.
P2: Habermas challenges them to write a 1,000-page book citing the same percentage of skeptics as he cites evangelicals.
P3: He allows them to include a few critiques, just as he occasionally includes critiques of conservatives.

st1.quote: Here's my challenge. Okay, you write a thousandpage book and have the same percentage of evangelicals that I have of skeptics.

st2.quote: You say you don't give critiques, you sneak in a few. Okay, you can sneak in a few of evangelicals, too.

st3.quote: Why don't we say, "Oh, so you quoted, I'll just make something up." Yeah, you've got 8,000ish footnotes, but I'm going to make it up.

st4.quote: I want to see who wears the skeptical work that cites as many of the conservatives nicely without same thing you critique me for without giving critiques.

st5.quote: I know it's just human nature to cite more people that agree with you.

st6.quote: But I want you to have the same percentage of treating evangelicals nicely and citing them in your work as of yours.

st7.quote: In fact, I have a running commentary on that in my own notes. I keep notes on it.

st8.quote: I think I'm quite fair in this volume.

or1.quote: Here's my challenge. Okay, you write a thousandpage book and have the same percentage of evangelicals that I have of skeptics.
or1.why: A tu quoque fairness challenge is not a restatement of a prior resurrection argument.

or2.quote: Yeah, you've got 8,000ish footnotes, but I'm going to make it up.
or2.why: It uses the 8,000-footnote figure but does not add new external evidence.

arguments.weakest_link: The challenge does not itself establish that Habermas's citation balance is fair.
arguments.develop_next: Publish the actual percentage breakdown of skeptical vs. friendly citations in volume 3.

arguments.name: No numerical threshold for 'highly evidenced'
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
arguments.conclusion: The first minimal-facts criterion, 'highly evidenced,' should not be reduced to a fixed percentage; it is better understood through categories of strong historical evidence.
premises: P1: Habermas has never counted scholars or assigned a percentage threshold except in his empty-tomb study.
P2: He measures evidence by categories such as multiple attestation, eyewitness testimony, and early sources.
P3: If he gave a number such as 80%, critics would misrepresent it as an arbitrary criterion.

st1.quote: But I do not have a certain threshold that they have to have to meet.

st2.quote: I'd say if I have multiple attestation, eyewitness and early sources, that's not a list of names. That's a list of categories.

st3.quote: When we do criteria we many many commentators have said that multiple attestation is the best evidence for documents multiple attestation.

st4.quote: So I would go for the stronger reasons, not the lesser reasons.

st5.quote: If I said, "Well, Dale, you give uh 51. I'd like at least 80." They're going to go, "See, he means 80."

st6.quote: But I don't have there. At no point do I ever say I need this many evidences.

st7.quote: I don't have any count to my recollection except the empty tomb.

st8.quote: I'd say if I have multiple attestation, eyewitness and early sources, that's not a list of names. That's a list of categories.

arguments.prior_art: Gary Habermas, minimal facts method, The Historical Jesus, 1996

or1.quote: But I do not have a certain threshold that they have to have to meet.
or1.why: It clarifies the existing minimal-facts criterion rather than offering a new argument.

or2.quote: I'd say if I have multiple attestation, eyewitness and early sources, that's not a list of names. That's a list of categories.
or2.why: It names categories of evidence but these are standard historiographical criteria already used in the prior art.

arguments.weakest_link: The rejection of numerical thresholds leaves 'highly evidenced' vague and hard to test.
arguments.develop_next: Specify a concrete decision rule for when the category-based evidence is sufficient.

arguments.name: Non-evangelical scholars support the minimal facts
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
arguments.conclusion: The minimal facts are strongly supported even by non-evangelical and skeptical scholars, which strengthens the case that they are not merely Christian bias.
premises: P1: James D. G. Dunn, a non-evangelical, holds that the resurrection preaching and creedal statements may go back within months of the crucifixion.
P2: Gerd Lüdemann, an atheist New Testament scholar, says the preaching of the resurrection began immediately.
P3: Bart Ehrman concedes it is a historical fact that the disciples thought they saw the risen Jesus.
P4: Dale Allison says the minimal facts approach is the best apologetical argument and that his skeptical approach does not deny any of the minimal facts.

st5.quote: But he said it's the best of the arguments and my approach, my skeptical approach, doesn't deny any of them.

or1.quote: So, if I have non-eangelicals saying those things, that that interests me

arguments.name: Scholarly consensus alone is not sufficient
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
arguments.conclusion: The scholarly-consensus criterion is not by itself sufficient for rational belief; the evidence criterion is far more important.
premises: P1: Habermas says criterion one is by far the more important of the two, perhaps 85-90% of the case.
P2: If the second criterion disappeared, one would be no worse off than other ancient historians.
P3: Scholarly consensus can be wrong if it is based on bias or social pressure.
